title: 2-Yoneda lemma
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, especially category theory, the 2-Yoneda lemma is a generalization of the Yoneda lemma to 2-categories. Precisely, given a contravariant pseudofunctor $F$ on a category C, it says: for each object $x$ in C, the natural functor (evaluation at the identity)
statement: Assume $F$ is a contravariant pseudofunctor on a category $C$; $x$ is an object of $C$; $h_x=\operatorname{Hom}_C(-,x)$. Evaluation at the identity is an equivalence of categories $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(h_x,F)\simeq F(x)$.
hypotheses: $F$ is a contravariant pseudofunctor on a category $C$
conclusions: Evaluation at the identity is an equivalence of categories $\underline{\operatorname{Hom}}(h_x,F)\simeq F(x)$.

title: Abel's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let the Taylor series $G(x)=\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }a_{k}x^{k}$ be a power series with real coefficients $a_{k}$ . Suppose that the series $\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }a_{k}$ converges. Then $G(x)$ is continuous from the left at $x=1,$ that is, $\lim _{x\to 1^{-}}G(x)=\sum _{k=0}^{\infty }a_{k}.$
statement: Assume $G(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_kx^k$ is a real-coefficient power series; $\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k$ converges. $\lim_{x\to1^-}G(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k$; equivalently, the power series extends continuously from the left to $x=1$.
conclusions: $\lim_{x\to1^-}G(x)=\sum_{k=0}^{\infty}a_k$; equivalently, the power series extends continuously from the left to $x=1$.
editorial_note: Uses the explicit real-variable theorem; complex Stolz-sector variant left as source context.

title: Adian–Rabin theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let P be a Markov property of finitely presentable groups. Then there does not exist an algorithm that, given a finite presentation $G=\langle X\mid R\rangle $ , decides whether or not the group $G$ defined by this presentation has property P.
statement: Assume $P$ is an isomorphism-invariant property of finitely presentable groups; Some finitely presentable group has property $P$; There exists a finitely presentable group which cannot embed in any finitely presentable group with property $P$. There is no algorithm which decides from an arbitrary finite group presentation whether the presented group has property $P$.
hypotheses: $P$ is an isomorphism-invariant property of finitely presentable groups
Some finitely presentable group has property $P$
There exists a finitely presentable group which cannot embed in any finitely presentable group with property $P$
conclusions: There is no algorithm which decides from an arbitrary finite group presentation whether the presented group has property $P$.

title: Apollonius's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In any triangle $ABC,$ if $AD$ is a median ( $|BD|=|CD|$ ), then $|AB|^{2}+|AC|^{2}=2(|BD|^{2}+|AD|^{2}).$ It is a special case of Stewart's theorem. For an isosceles triangle with $|AB|=|AC|,$ the median $AD$ is perpendicular to $BC$ and the theorem reduces to the Pythagorean theorem for triangle $ADB$ (or triangle $ADC$ ). From the fact that the diagonals of a parallelogram bisect each other, the theorem is equivalent to the parallelogram law.
statement: Assume $ABC$ is a triangle; $D$ is the midpoint of side $BC$. $|AB|^2+|AC|^2=2(|BD|^2+|AD|^2)$.

title: Ax–Grothendieck theorem
source_statement_excerpt: The theorem is often given as this special case: If $P$ is an injective polynomial function from an $n$ -dimensional complex vector space to itself then $P$ is bijective. That is, if $P$ always maps distinct arguments to distinct values, then the values of $P$ cover all of $\mathbb {C} ^{n}$ .

title: Büchi–Elgot–Trakhtenbrot theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In formal language theory, the Büchi–Elgot–Trakhtenbrot theorem states that a language is regular if and only if it can be defined by a formula in monadic second-order logic (MSO). The theorem is due to Julius Richard Büchi, Calvin Elgot, and Boris Trakhtenbrot.
statement: Assume $L$ is a language of finite words over a finite alphabet. $L$ is regular if and only if $L$ is definable in monadic second-order logic over words.
hypotheses: $L$ is a language of finite words over a finite alphabet
conclusions: $L$ is regular if and only if $L$ is definable in monadic second-order logic over words.

title: Basu's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $(P_{\theta };\theta \in \Theta )$ be a family of distributions on a measurable space $(X,{\mathcal {A}})$ and a statistic $T$ maps from $(X,{\mathcal {A}})$ to some measurable space $(Y,{\mathcal {B}})$ . If $T$ is a boundedly complete sufficient statistic for $\theta $ , and $A$ is ancillary to $\theta $ , then conditional on $\theta $ , $T$ is independent of $A$ . That is, $T\perp \!\!\!\perp A\mid \theta $ .
statement: Assume $(P_\theta)_{\theta\in\Theta}$ is a statistical model; $T$ is a boundedly complete sufficient statistic; $A$ is an ancillary statistic. $T$ and $A$ are independent under each $P_\theta$.
hypotheses: $T$ is a boundedly complete sufficient statistic
conclusions: $T$ and $A$ are independent under each $P_\theta$.
editorial_note: Statement expressed as independence under each model distribution.

title: Beckman–Quarles theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Formally, the result is as follows. Let $f$ be a function or multivalued function from a $d$ -dimensional Euclidean space to itself, and suppose that, for every pair of points $p$ and $q$ that are at unit distance from each other, every pair of images $f(p)$ and $f(q)$ are also at unit distance from each other. Then $f$ must be an isometry: it is a one-to-one function that preserves distances between all pairs of points.
statement: Assume $d\ge2$; $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ maps every pair of points at Euclidean distance 1 to a pair at distance 1. $f$ preserves all Euclidean distances and is an isometry.
hypotheses: $f:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ maps every pair of points at Euclidean distance 1 to a pair at distance 1
conclusions: $f$ preserves all Euclidean distances and is an isometry.

title: Blakers–Massey theorem
source_statement_excerpt: In mathematics, the first Blakers–Massey theorem, named after Albert Blakers and William S. Massey, gave vanishing conditions for certain triad homotopy groups of spaces.

conclusions: The map of pairs $(A,C)\to(X,B)$ induces isomorphisms on relative homotopy groups in degrees $k\le m+n-1$, and a surjection in degree $k=m+n$.

It is named after the Indian mathematician Brahmagupta (598-668).

title: Brouwer fixed-point theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Brouwer's fixed-point theorem is a fixed-point theorem in topology, named after L. E. J. Brouwer. It states that for any continuous function $f$ mapping a nonempty compact convex set to itself, there is a point $x_{0}$ such that $f(x_{0})=x_{0}$ . The simplest forms of Brouwer's theorem are for continuous functions $f$ from a closed interval $I$ in the real numbers to itself or from a closed disk $D$ to itself. A more general form than the latter is for continuous functions from a nonempty convex compact subset $K$ of Euclidean space to itself.
statement: Assume $K$ is a nonempty compact convex subset of a Euclidean space; $f:K\to K$ is continuous. There exists $x\in K$ with $f(x)=x$.
hypotheses: $K$ is a nonempty compact convex subset of a Euclidean space
conclusions: There exists $x\in K$ with $f(x)=x$.
editorial_note: Uses the finite-dimensional Euclidean statement, not the general Banach-space setting.

title: Budan's theorem
source_statement_excerpt: Let $c_{0},c_{1},c_{2},\ldots c_{k}$ be a finite sequence of real numbers. A sign variation or sign change in the sequence is a pair of indices i < j such that $c_{i}c_{j}<0,$ and either j = i + 1 or $c_{k}=0$ for all k such that i < k < j.

title: Carathéodory's theorem (convex hull)
source_statement_excerpt: Carathéodory's theorem is a theorem in convex geometry. It states that if a point $x$ lies in the convex hull $\mathrm {Conv} (P)$ of a set $P\subset \mathbb {R} ^{d}$ , then $x$ lies in some $d$ -dimensional simplex with vertices in $P$ . Equivalently, $x$ can be written as the convex combination of $d+1$ or fewer points in $P$ . Additionally, $x$ can be written as the convex combination of at most $d+1$ extremal points in $P$ , as non-extremal points can be removed from $P$ without changing the membership of $x$ in the convex hull.
statement: Assume $P\subseteq\mathbb R^d$; $x\in\operatorname{conv}(P)$. There are at most $d+1$ points $p_1,\dots,p_k\in P$ and nonnegative coefficients $\lambda_i$ summing to 1 such that $x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i p_i$.
conclusions: There are at most $d+1$ points $p_1,\dots,p_k\in P$ and nonnegative coefficients $\lambda_i$ summing to 1 such that $x=\sum_{i=1}^{k}\lambda_i p_i$.
editorial_note: Prepared standard convex-combination form; omitted source's additional extremal-points remark.

title: Cauchy's limit theorem
source_statement_excerpt: If the arithmetic means in Cauchy's limit theorem are replaced by weighted arithmetic means those converge as well. More precisely for sequence $(a_{n})$ with $a_{n}\to a$ and a sequence of positive real numbers $(p_{n})$ with ${\frac {1}{p_{1}+\cdots +p_{n}}}\to 0$ one has ${\frac {p_{1}a_{1}+\cdots +p_{n}a_{n}}{p_{1}+\cdots +p_{n}}}\to a$ .
statement: Assume $(a_n)$ is a convergent sequence of real or complex numbers with $a_n\to a$. Its arithmetic means converge to the same limit: $\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\to a$.
hypotheses: $(a_n)$ is a convergent sequence of real or complex numbers with $a_n\to a$
conclusions: Its arithmetic means converge to the same limit: $\frac{a_1+\cdots+a_n}{n}\to a$.
